title: Slater winners
description: The Slater winners: the candidates that head a ranking that goes against the fewest majority preferences, whatever their margins (Theta-2-complete, Lampis 2022). The loop is core-guided (OLL: Andres, Kaufmann, Matheis and Schaub 2012; Morgado, Dodaro and Marques-Silva 2014): each unsat core is a cycle of majority preferences or a totaliser output, which raises the lower bound by one; once a ranking exists, the assumptions left describe exactly the Slater rankings, and one more query per candidate finds the winners. The fragments are those of kemeny-winners with unit weights; compare OLL with that example's implicit hitting sets on the F1 seasons.
readme:
# Project: Slater winners

## Research question

Slater's rule (Slater 1961) counts the majority preferences a ranking goes against, all with
weight 1; its winner problem is Theta-2-complete (Lampis 2022). With unit
weights, many hitting sets of the cycles found so far are optimal, and implicit hitting sets
struggle; core-guided search raises the bound one core at a time. How large is the gap on real
elections, and what does the per-candidate query cost?

## The loops

- **default**: OLL (Andres et al. 2012; Morgado et al. 2014). C is asked under "every majority preference is kept"; each unsat core raises
  the lower bound by one and is replaced by totaliser outputs. When C has a model, the assumptions
  left describe exactly the Slater rankings: one more query per candidate (its being first) decides
  whether it is a winner. That is the Theta-2 pattern: an optimum, then one round of NP queries.
- **plain-cores**: OLL with the cores as clasp returns them.
- **ihs**: the implicit hitting set loop of kemeny-winners, with unit weights.
- **lazy-transitivity**: 3-cycles added lazily to an order of every pair.
- **reference**: rankings blocked one by one (small instances only).

## Baseline

Time of a run with all solutions on clingo-wasm (`tools/bench.mjs`, suite `loops`, limit 60 s, two runs at a time) and, in brackets, the refinements added, counting the blocks that rule out a winner. The small instances take under 0.2 s with every loop.

| instance | default | plain-cores | ihs | lazy-transitivity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1964: 9 drivers | 0.0 s (11) | 0.1 s (11) | 0.0 s (12) | 0.0 s (16) |
| 1970: 9 drivers | 0.0 s (12) | 0.0 s (12) | 0.0 s (13) | 0.0 s (13) |
| 1978: 20 drivers | 0.3 s (31) | 0.3 s (31) | 27.1 s (49) | 22.9 s (46) |
| 1993: 23 drivers | 0.6 s (38) | 1.4 s (38) | > 60 s | > 60 s |
| 1991: 31 drivers | 1.7 s (47) | 21.4 s (47) | > 60 s | > 60 s |
| Latin square: 5, 65 voters | 0.0 s (8) | 0.0 s (8) | 0.0 s (11) | 0.0 s (9) |

With unit weights the implicit hitting sets of the cycles have many optima, and each round of the ihs variant pays for a hard optimal solve of A; OLL needs one cheap call per core and a query per candidate (31 drivers in 1.7 s).

## Things to try

- The 1991 season (`f1-1991`, 31 drivers): OLL finds Mansell in about 2 s; the hitting sets and
  lazy transitivity do not finish in two minutes.
- Weighted OLL for Kemeny (weights split into unit copies, as in `maxsat-oll-weighted`): does it
  beat the hitting sets of kemeny-winners?
- Stratification: relax the cores through the winner's own preferences first.

## How to measure

Each suite runs its variants on the instances (Campaign tab, Advanced mode); headless:
`node tools/bench.mjs slater-winners --suite loops --out rows.jsonl` and `node tools/report.mjs rows.jsonl`.
The instances tagged `slow` (the larger F1 seasons and the Latin square) are where the loops differ;
the small ones are for the audit (`node tools/audit.mjs slater-winners --instance all --variant ihs`) and the tests.
The suite `mallows` draws elections of 6 to 10 candidates. Every expected count was checked
against an independent encoding with clingo's own optimisation, or by brute force on the small ones.

## References

- P. Slater. Inconsistencies in a schedule of paired comparisons. *Biometrika* 48(3/4):303–312, 1961.
- M. Lampis. Determining a Slater winner is complete for parallel access to NP. *STACS 2022*, LIPIcs 219, paper 45.
- B. Andres, B. Kaufmann, O. Matheis and T. Schaub. Unsatisfiability-based optimization in clasp. *ICLP 2012 (Technical Communications)*, LIPIcs 17, 211–221.
- A. Morgado, C. Dodaro and J. Marques-Silva. Core-guided MaxSAT with soft cardinality constraints. *CP 2014*, LNCS 8656, 564–573.
- J. Davies and F. Bacchus. Solving MAXSAT by solving a sequence of simpler SAT instances. *CP 2011*, LNCS 6876, 225–239.
- V. Conitzer, A. Davenport and J. Kalagnanam. Improved bounds for computing Kemeny rankings. *AAAI 2006*, 620–626.
- N. Mattei and T. Walsh. PrefLib: a library for preferences. *ADT 2013*, LNCS 8176, 259–270. Data: dataset 00052 (Formula 1 seasons), https://www.preflib.org.

fragments.name: shared
fragments.text:
% The election is the instance (Instances tab). ballot(V,(A,B,...)): voter V ranks A first,
% B second, and so on; count(V,N) (optional): N voters cast this ballot, as in PrefLib's
% "N: a,b,...". Ballots of 3 to 12 candidates are read below; for more, give rank(V,P,X).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F;V,7,G) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F,G)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F;V,7,G;V,8,H) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F;V,7,G;V,8,H;V,9,I) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F;V,7,G;V,8,H;V,9,I;V,10,J) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F;V,7,G;V,8,H;V,9,I;V,10,J;V,11,K) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J,K)).
rank(V,1,A;V,2,B;V,3,C;V,4,D;V,5,E;V,6,F;V,7,G;V,8,H;V,9,I;V,10,J;V,11,K;V,12,L) :- ballot(V,(A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I,J,K,L)).
% rank(V,P,X): voter V puts candidate X in place P.
cand(X) :- rank(_,_,X).
#defined count/2.
votes(V,N) :- rank(V,1,_), N = #max { 1; M : count(V,M) }.
% n(X,Y,N): N voters prefer X to Y.
n(X,Y,N) :- cand(X), cand(Y), X != Y, N = #sum { W,V : rank(V,I,X), rank(V,J,Y), I < J, votes(V,W) }.
% edge(X,Y,M): a majority prefers X to Y, by a margin of M votes.
edge(X,Y,N-K) :- n(X,Y,N), n(Y,X,K), N > K.
% Slater: a ranking pays one for every majority preference it goes against, whatever the
% margin (only the majority relation counts). So every w/3 is 1.
w(X,Y,1) :- edge(X,Y,_).
fragments.description: The election: pairwise counts, the majority relation and the weights w/3 of the rule. Added to every solver.

fragments.name: hitting
fragments.text:
% A candidate: the winner, which the ranking puts first, and the majority preferences that the
% ranking goes against (rev). The refinements say which ones must be reversed.
1 { top(X) : cand(X) } 1.
{ rev(X,Y) : edge(X,Y,_) }.
% The cost: the weights of the reversed majority preferences.
#minimize { W,X,Y : rev(X,Y), w(X,Y,W) }.
#show top/1.
#show rev/2.
fragments.description: Solver A: a winner and the majority preferences to reverse, of least total weight.

fragments.name: first
fragments.text:
% The winner is ranked first, so every majority that prefers another candidate to it is
% reversed. (The OLL loop of slater-winners leaves this fragment out: its first model must
% reverse nothing.)
rev(X,Y) :- top(Y), edge(X,Y,_).
fragments.description: Solver A of the variant ihs: the winner is first, so the majorities against it are reversed.

fragments.name: glue
fragments.text:
% The check reads which majority preferences the candidate reverses.
glue(rev(X,Y)) :- edge(X,Y,_).
fragments.description: Link G: the reversed majority preferences.

fragments.name: glue_top
fragments.text:
% The winner, on a link of its own: W.block(M) rules out a winner, W(M) assumes it.
glue(top(X)) :- cand(X).

fragments.name: order
fragments.text:
% A ranking (above/2: a strict linear order of the candidates) ...
{ above(X,Y) } :- cand(X), cand(Y), X < Y.
above(Y,X) :- cand(X), cand(Y), X < Y, not above(X,Y).
:- above(X,Y), above(Y,Z), above(Z,X).
% ... that puts the winner first, when the loop assumes one (link W) ...
:- top(X), above(Y,X).
% ... and keeps every majority preference the candidate does not reverse. There is none
% exactly when the kept preferences contain a cycle; a minimal unsat core is such a cycle.
:- edge(X,Y,_), not rev(X,Y), not above(X,Y).
place(X,N+1) :- cand(X), N = #count { Y : above(Y,X) }.
#show place/2.

% OLL (the default loop). The soft constraints are "rev(X,Y) is false" and the totaliser
% outputs added by relax; viol(T) says that soft constraint T is violated.
viol(rev(X,Y)) :- rev(X,Y).

#program relax(k).
% core(k,T): the k-th unsat core (a cycle of majority preferences, or later a mix of
% preferences and totaliser outputs), one fact per soft constraint in it. Every ranking
% violates at least one of them: that is the +1 of the lower bound. over(k,J) says that at
% least J are violated; each over(k,J) for J >= 2 becomes a new soft constraint.
size(k,N) :- N = #count { T : core(k,T) }.
over(k,J) :- size(k,N), J = 2..N, #count { T : core(k,T), viol(T) } >= J.
viol(over(k,J)) :- over(k,J).
fragments.description: Solver C: a ranking that keeps every majority preference not reversed; the totalisers of OLL.

fragments.name: tournament
fragments.text:
% A candidate: a winner and an order of every pair of candidates (a tournament), which need
% not be transitive: the check finds the cycles, and each refinement removes one.
1 { top(X) : cand(X) } 1.
{ above(X,Y) } :- cand(X), cand(Y), X < Y.
above(Y,X) :- cand(X), cand(Y), X < Y, not above(X,Y).
:- top(X), above(Y,X).
% The cost: the weights of the majority preferences the order goes against.
#minimize { W,X,Y : w(X,Y,W), above(Y,X) }.
#show top/1.
fragments.description: Solver A of the variant lazy-transitivity: a winner and an order of every pair, of least weight.

fragments.name: triangle
fragments.text:
% A counterexample: three candidates that the order puts in a cycle. A ranking orders a
% triple transitively, so one of the three pairs must turn round.
1 { cyc(X,Y,Z) : cand(X), cand(Y), cand(Z), X < Y, X < Z, Y != Z } 1.
:- cyc(X,Y,Z), not above(X,Y).
:- cyc(X,Y,Z), not above(Y,Z).
:- cyc(X,Y,Z), not above(Z,X).
relevant(above(X,Y)) :- cyc(X,Y,Z).
relevant(above(Y,Z)) :- cyc(X,Y,Z).
relevant(above(Z,X)) :- cyc(X,Y,Z).
#show cyc/3.
fragments.description: Solver C of the variant lazy-transitivity: three candidates in a cycle.

fragments.name: glue_above
fragments.text:
% The check reads the order of every pair.
glue(above(X,Y)) :- cand(X), cand(Y), X != Y.
fragments.description: Link G of the variants lazy-transitivity and reference: the order of every pair.

fragments.name: transitive
fragments.text:
% The blocking loop's candidates are rankings: the order is transitive.
:- above(X,Y), above(Y,Z), above(Z,X).
fragments.description: Solver A of the variant reference: the order is a ranking.

fragments.name: better
fragments.text:
% A counterexample: another ranking r/2, with any winner, that goes against majority
% preferences of a smaller total weight than the candidate's ranking.
{ r(X,Y) } :- cand(X), cand(Y), X < Y.
r(Y,X) :- cand(X), cand(Y), X < Y, not r(X,Y).
:- r(X,Y), r(Y,Z), r(Z,X).
:- #sum { W,X,Y : w(X,Y,W), r(Y,X) ; -W,X,Y : w(X,Y,W), above(Y,X) } >= 0.
#show r/2.
fragments.description: Solver C of the variant reference: a ranking that goes against less.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + hitting
solver C = shared + order
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue
link   W = A -> C via shared + glue_top

# Core-guided optimisation (OLL: Andres, Kaufmann, Matheis and Schaub 2012; Morgado, Dodaro
# and Marques-Silva 2014), then one query per
# candidate: the Theta-2 pattern of an optimum followed by a final round of NP queries.
# Phase 1: C is called under the assumptions "every majority preference is kept". Each unsat
# core is a cycle (later also totaliser outputs): the lower bound goes up by one, the core is
# relaxed and replaced by the outputs over(k,J) of a totaliser, assumed false.
M = A.solve(optimal)               # a winner, and no majority preference reversed
E = G(M)
lower = 0
loop:
    track lower = lower
    X = C.solve(assume E)
    if X: break
    K = C.core.minimal
    lower = lower + 1
    count cores
    for a in K:                    # relax the core's soft constraints
        E = E.without(a)
    C.expand(relax, core = K)      # facts core(k,T): the core's soft constraints
    j = 2
    while j <= K.size:             # the new soft constraints: not over(k,j)
        o = C.atom("over", C.step, j)
        for a in o:
            E.push(a)
            E = E.flip(a)
        j = j + 1
log "Slater score", lower
# Phase 2: OLL keeps the number of reversed preferences of every model of C equal to lower
# plus the assumptions of E it violates. So the models of C under E are exactly the Slater
# rankings, and a candidate is a Slater winner exactly when C has a model under E with it
# first. A proposes the candidates; each is ruled out after its query.
loop:
    if C.solve(assume E, W(M)):
        log "Slater winner", M.value(top/1), "score", lower
        accept M
    A.add(W.block(M))
    M = A.solve(optimal)               # the next candidate, again reversing nothing
    if not M: stop

% Eight voters, five candidates, no Condorcet winner: the majority prefers b to e, e to d and
% d to b. The four rules of the Voting group pick four different sets of winners here.
ballot(1,(e,d,b,a,c)).  count(1,3).
ballot(2,(b,e,d,c,a)).
ballot(3,(a,d,b,e,c)).
ballot(4,(d,b,c,a,e)).
ballot(5,(a,b,e,c,d)).  count(5,2).

% The Condorcet paradox: each candidate loses to another one two votes to one, so every
% rule ties all three.
ballot(1,(a,b,c)).
ballot(2,(b,c,a)).
ballot(3,(c,a,b)).

% A Condorcet winner, b, which beats every other candidate head to head although a and c have
% more first places. All four rules pick it alone.
ballot(1,(a,b,c,d)).  count(1,2).
ballot(2,(c,b,d,a)).  count(2,2).
ballot(3,(b,d,a,c)).

% Eleven voters, five candidates. Kemeny picks e, Slater a, Dodgson c and e, Young d and e.

ballot(3,(c,a,b,d,e)).

ballot(8,(b,a,c,e,d)).  count(8,2).

generators.name: election-mallows
generators.description: v voters over the first m of the candidates a..j, each ranking them by a Mallows model around a, b, c, ... with dispersion phi/1000 (1000 = impartial culture).
generators.text:
% election-mallows: v voters over the candidates a, b, c, ... (the first m, at most 10); voter V
% puts candidate I in place @mallows(m, phi, I, V) of a Mallows ranking around a, b, c, ...
% (dispersion phi/1000: 0 = everyone agrees, 1000 = impartial culture).
name(1,a;2,b;3,c;4,d;5,e;6,f;7,g;8,h;9,i;10,j).
voter(1..v).
rank(V,@mallows(m,phi,I,V),X) :- voter(V), name(I,X), I <= m.
#show rank/3.

generators.name: election-latin
generators.description: A Latin square: the m cyclic shifts of the ranking a, b, c, ..., each cast by lo to hi voters. No Condorcet winner unless the counts are lopsided; large Dodgson and Young scores.
generators.text:
% election-latin: the m cyclic shifts of the ranking a, b, c, ... (m at most 10), shift S cast
% by @int(lo, hi, S) voters. Every candidate is in every place once, so the counts decide.
name(1,a;2,b;3,c;4,d;5,e;6,f;7,g;8,h;9,i;10,j).
shift(0..m-1).
rank(S+1,P,X) :- shift(S), P = 1..m, name(I,X), I = (P - 1 + S) \ m + 1.
count(S+1,@int(lo,hi,S)) :- shift(S).
#show rank/3.
#show count/2.

variants.name: plain-cores
variants.note: OLL with the cores as clasp returns them (C.core): longer cores, larger totalisers.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + hitting
solver C = shared + order
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue
link   W = A -> C via shared + glue_top

# Core-guided optimisation (OLL: Andres, Kaufmann, Matheis and Schaub 2012; Morgado, Dodaro
# and Marques-Silva 2014), then one query per
# candidate: the Theta-2 pattern of an optimum followed by a final round of NP queries.
# Phase 1: C is called under the assumptions "every majority preference is kept". Each unsat
# core is a cycle (later also totaliser outputs): the lower bound goes up by one, the core is
# relaxed and replaced by the outputs over(k,J) of a totaliser, assumed false.
M = A.solve(optimal)               # a winner, and no majority preference reversed
E = G(M)
lower = 0
loop:
    track lower = lower
    X = C.solve(assume E)
    if X: break
    K = C.core
    lower = lower + 1
    count cores
    for a in K:                    # relax the core's soft constraints
        E = E.without(a)
    C.expand(relax, core = K)      # facts core(k,T): the core's soft constraints
    j = 2
    while j <= K.size:             # the new soft constraints: not over(k,j)
        o = C.atom("over", C.step, j)
        for a in o:
            E.push(a)
            E = E.flip(a)
        j = j + 1
log "Slater score", lower
# Phase 2: OLL keeps the number of reversed preferences of every model of C equal to lower
# plus the assumptions of E it violates. So the models of C under E are exactly the Slater
# rankings, and a candidate is a Slater winner exactly when C has a model under E with it
# first. A proposes the candidates; each is ruled out after its query.
loop:
    if C.solve(assume E, W(M)):
        log "Slater winner", M.value(top/1), "score", lower
        accept M
    A.add(W.block(M))
    M = A.solve(optimal)               # the next candidate, again reversing nothing
    if not M: stop

variants.name: ihs
variants.note: Implicit hitting sets (the default loop of kemeny-winners) with unit weights: optimal hitting sets of the cycles found.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + hitting + first
solver C = shared + order
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue
link   W = A -> C via shared + glue_top

# Implicit hitting sets (MaxHS: Davies and Bacchus 2011) for the Slater winners. A best
# ranking goes against a cheapest set of majority preferences that meets every cycle of the
# majority graph (a minimum feedback arc set); the cycles are generated lazily, as in
# Baharev, Schichl, Neumaier and Achterberg (2021). A proposes a winner and a cheapest set of
# majority preferences to go against that meets every cycle found so far; its cost is a lower
# bound for that winner. C looks for a ranking that keeps all the other majority preferences.
# Found: the bound is the score. The first winner found has the best score; another winner is
# one whose bound reaches no more than that.
best = none
loop:
    M = A.solve(optimal)
    if not M: stop
    track lower = M.cost
    if best != none and M.cost > best:
        A.add(W.block(M))                # its bound already exceeds the best score: not a winner
        continue
    X = C.solve(assume G(M))
    if X:
        log "Slater winner", M.value(top/1), "score", M.cost
        accept M
        best = M.cost
        A.add(W.block(M))                # look for the next winner
    else:
        # a minimal unsat core is a cycle of kept majority preferences (an MUS):
        # the ranking must go against one of them
        A.add(C.core.minimal.on(G))
        count cycles

variants.name: lazy-transitivity
variants.note: The order of every pair at least cost, transitivity added lazily, one 3-cycle at a time (clauses from relevant/1).

loop.text:
solver A = shared + tournament
solver C = shared + triangle
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue_above
link   W = A -> C via shared + glue_top

# Lazy transitivity: the ordering formulation (one variable per pair, a constraint per
# 3-cycle; Conitzer, Davenport and Kalagnanam 2006) with the 3-cycle constraints added only
# when violated. A orders every pair at the least cost but without transitivity; C finds a triple in a cycle, and the clause from its three
# relevant pairs says that one of them must turn round. An order without a cycle is a ranking
# of least cost with this winner first.
best = none
loop:
    M = A.solve(optimal)
    if not M: stop
    track lower = M.cost
    if best != none and M.cost > best:
        A.add(W.block(M))                # this winner's least cost already exceeds the best
        continue
    X = C.solve(assume G(M))
    if X:
        A.add(G.clause(M, X))            # one pair of the cycle must turn round
        count triangles
    else:
        log "Slater winner", M.value(top/1), "score", M.cost
        accept M
        best = M.cost
        A.add(W.block(M))

variants.name: reference
variants.note: The blocking loop: rankings with the winner first, each refuted ranking blocked on its own. Small instances only.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + tournament + transitive
solver C = shared + better
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue_above
link   W = A -> C via shared + glue_top

# The blocking loop: A proposes a winner and a ranking with the winner first; C looks for a
# ranking that goes against less (any winner). A refuted ranking is blocked on its own; a
# ranking without a better one makes its first candidate a Slater winner, which is then ruled out.
loop:
    M = A.solve()
    if not M: stop
    X = C.solve(assume G(M))
    if X:
        A.add(G.block(M))
    else:
        accept M
        A.add(W.block(M))

library.summary: Slater winners by core-guided optimisation (OLL), then one query per candidate on the reformulated problem (8 voters, 3 winners); F1 seasons from PrefLib; variants with implicit hitting sets and lazy transitivity.
